title: \(\exists\mathbb{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}\)
formal:
Is \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{NP}\) in the ordinary bit-cost Turing model? Equivalently, is truth of every finitely encoded existential sentence over the ordered real field certifiable by a polynomial-length binary string checked in deterministic polynomial time?

For the language ETR defined below, the concrete target is the existence of one deterministic Turing verifier \(V\) and polynomial bounds \(p,q\) such that, for every binary string \(u\),
\[u\in\mathrm{ETR}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|u|)}:\ V(u,w)=1,\]
with \(V\) halting within \(q(|u|)\) steps on every permitted pair. The question is unconditional and has no oracle or advice.
definitions:
ETR is a language of finite binary strings describing sentences
\[\exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R:\ \Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_m).\]
Here \(m\ge0\), the entire list of quantified variables is written explicitly, and \(\Phi\) is an explicitly listed finite Boolean formula, using \(\land,\lor,\neg\) and parentheses, whose atomic predicates are \(p=0\) or \(p>0\). Boolean constants true and false are permitted. Each polynomial is a finite monomial list
\[p(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{j=1}^{s}c_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}x_i^{e_{ij}},\qquad c_j\in\mathbb Z,\quad e_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.\]
Every coefficient is a signed binary integer and every exponent is a nonnegative binary integer. Each monomial has its coefficient and its full exponent vector, explicitly delimited. Zero coefficients and repeated monomials are allowed with their usual algebraic meaning. The empty sum is zero and the empty product is one. The convention \(x^0=1\) applies also at \(x=0\). No degree bound is imposed.

Use a fixed finite-alphabet, explicitly delimited encoding of the variable declarations, formula tree, monomial lists, signs and binary integers, then a fixed binary encoding of its symbols. Variable names are indices from 1 through \(m\); no implicit generation of an exponentially long formula is allowed. Let \(L=|u|\) be the entire encoding length, counting every bit of every coefficient and exponent as well as all syntactic structure. Ill-formed strings, invalid indices and unmatched lengths are rejected. With no quantified variables, the sentence has its ordinary closed-form truth value. Inequalities such as \(p\le0\) and comparisons between two polynomials can be expressed with the stated atoms and connectives.

A well-formed string is in ETR precisely when there exists an exact real tuple satisfying its sentence. There is no numerical tolerance or robustness promise. The reals occur as mathematical values of the quantified variables, not as infinite objects supplied to a Turing machine. Binary exponents and coefficients are counted by their bit lengths. This explicit sparse-polynomial representation is polynomially interreducible with the standard arithmetic-term definition of ETR; it does not encode an exponentially long formula by a separate succinct circuit description.

For languages \(A,B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), a polynomial-time many-one reduction is one total function \(f\) computed by a deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in \(|u|\), such that \(u\in A\) if and only if \(f(u)\in B\). Define \(\exists\mathbb R\) as all languages with such a reduction to ETR. A language is \(\exists\mathbb R\)-complete when it lies in that class and every language of the class reduces to it in this sense.

NP consists of languages with a single deterministic polynomial-time Turing verifier and polynomial-length binary witnesses. The program and polynomial bounds are fixed independently of the instance and its length. A verifier must reject every allowed witness on a no-instance and accept at least one on every yes-instance. Every finite-alphabet tape transition costs one; arithmetic on large integers and manipulation of algebraic descriptions are charged their actual bit cost. There is no randomness, oracle, nonuniform advice or exact-real primitive. A witness may encode any finite mathematical certificate with an efficiently checkable interpretation: it need not list a satisfying coordinate tuple or use rational coordinates.

The known inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\exists\mathbb R\), and closure of NP under these reductions, make class equality equivalent to \(\mathrm{ETR}\in\mathrm{NP}\). Its negation is \(\mathrm{ETR}\notin\mathrm{NP}\). The other known upper bound uses PSPACE, the class decidable by deterministic Turing machines using polynomially many work-tape cells.

For comparison, a constant-free BSS verifier stores exact reals and performs field operations and order tests at unit cost, using only the fixed constants 0 and 1. Restricting its input to bits while allowing polynomially many real witness coordinates gives \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}^{0})=\exists\mathbb R\). In the full BSS class comparison, inputs and finitely many fixed machine constants may also be arbitrary reals. That is a different target. The present question asks whether ordinary binary certificates with a bit-cost verifier suffice.

context_blocks.text: Geometric realizations and continuous constraints naturally supply real-valued witnesses. For example, \(\exists x\in\mathbb R:\ x^2=2\) is true and has no rational solution, while \(\exists x\in\mathbb R:\ x^2+1=0\) is false. The first example nevertheless has an elementary finite certificate; irrationality alone is no obstruction to membership in NP.

The established containments are \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\exists\mathbb R\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\). The lower inclusion comes from expressing Boolean constraints over the reals, and the upper inclusion is a theorem about ordinary polynomial space. Neither containment is known to be strict in the May 2026 source.

The class unifies many geometric recognition and realization problems, including stretchability of pseudoline arrangements and variants of the art-gallery problem. Equality with NP would give ordinary polynomially checkable certificates for every complete problem; separation would establish a limitation shared by all such complete problems.

The 2025 structural paper proves opposite oracle behaviors in its specified real-machine oracle model. Its oracle is a subset of \(\mathbb R^{*}\), and the real verifier may ask about arbitrary real tuples, whereas a Turing machine can only construct finite discrete queries. In particular, an exact integer-membership oracle creates a separation in that enlarged model. These results do not determine the unrelativized classes, and should not be read as a separation using identical finite-string query capabilities.

The same paper proves a conditional analogue of Ladner’s theorem: if \(\exists\mathbb R\ne\mathrm{NP}\), then some problem belongs to \(\exists\mathbb R\setminus\mathrm{NP}\) without being \(\exists\mathbb R\)-complete. The hypothesis is the unresolved comparison, rather than a consequence of the theorem.

The March 2026 tutorial restates the machine characterization using finite binary inputs, real witnesses and restricted constants. Its real verifier checks exact arithmetic at unit cost, so the characterization does not provide a polynomial-time bit-cost NP verifier.

A May 2026 preprint reports a probabilistically checkable proof theorem with real-valued proof entries and a verifier using exact real operations. It also reports obstacles to short coordinate descriptions even for some approximate solutions. Those are different guarantees from a polynomial-length binary certificate checked in polynomial bit time; the preprint explicitly leaves the NP comparison unresolved.

why: The answer would decide whether a broad class of geometric and algebraic existence problems has ordinary efficiently checkable finite certificates. It tests the boundary between discrete verification and exact continuous witnesses, with consequences across every problem complete for the existential theory of the reals.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{ETR}\in\mathrm{NP}\) or of \(\mathrm{ETR}\notin\mathrm{NP}\) for the encoding and model above, equivalently proving or refuting \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer must supply a uniform binary-certificate verification scheme and prove completeness, soundness, a polynomial certificate-length bound and a polynomial bit-time bound for all instances. A negative answer must exclude every such scheme. Showing only that some solutions are irrational, that a chosen coordinate representation needs many bits, or that a particular geometric problem is NP-hard does not exclude other certificate encodings. An oracle separation or a theorem conditional on unequal classes does not settle this unrelativized comparison. The decision target is exact, without numerical approximation tolerance.

progress.text: The compendium states the class definition, its machine characterization and the open \(\mathrm{NP}\) comparison.
The structural preprint gives oracle variants and a conditional intermediate-problem theorem; it does not assert an unrelativized separation.
The tutorial distinguishes discrete input and reduction cost from the real-valued witness-verification model.
The real-PCP preprint explicitly states that strictness of the NP lower inclusion and PSPACE upper inclusion remains unknown. Its real-valued proof result does not establish NP membership.

status_note: Explicitly unresolved in the checked 2024 compendium, February 2025 structural preprint and May 2026 PCP preprint. On 16 September 2026 the review read the exact formula and machine conventions, the oracle-query caveat, the conditional intermediate-problem statement and the 2026 real-verifier scope. Bounded subsequent-result searches found no established unrelativized equality or separation. The recent preprint proofs were not independently checked in full, and this literature review is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

sentences: The existential theory of the reals asks whether a finite system of polynomial conditions has an exact real solution.
Its input is a binary formula, with all coefficient and exponent bits counted in the running-time measure.
The question is whether every yes-instance has a polynomial-length binary certificate checked in ordinary polynomial time.
Known containments, oracle results and real-valued proof systems leave that discrete-certificate question unresolved in the checked sources.
A complete answer must establish or refute ETR membership in NP without restricting possible certificate representations.
